utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And good morning, everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Kapila Waidyaratne, assisted by Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start with today's witness, as time is of essence, I have to announce the following decision. It's the order to the Registry of the Tribunal to provide documents from the 5th of July. This Trial Chamber II of the International Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the Territory of the Former Yugoslavia since 1991 ("International Tribunal"). Being seized of a motion filed by the Office of the Prosecutor on 2nd of July, 2002, seeking an order for subpoena duces tecum to the United Nations Detention Unit to provide: (1) original records or documents in the form of receipts, requests, medical records, and letters signed or handwritten by Milomir Stakic since his detention, but not to include any communications to or from Defence counsel or Defence counsel investigators;. (2) original documents such as driver's license, passport, or similar documents that were in the possession of Milomir Stakic upon his arrival at the Detention Unit. Noting that the Defence counsel for Dr. Stakic have contested the authenticity of signatures alleged to be those of Dr. Stakic, which appear on a number of documentary exhibits tendered by the Prosecution in its case. Noting the order of 28 June, 2002, issued by this Chamber to the Prosecution to appoint a forensic handwriting examiner to assess the question whether the signatures which appear on the signed documents are those of Dr. Stakic, as the Prosecution contends. Noting that the Defence indicated in open Court that Dr. Stakic had chosen to exercise his right not to provide a sample of his handwriting to the Prosecution. Noting that the Prosecution in its motion submits that comparative material "would be helpful" in relation to any analysis of the signatures which appear on the signed documents. Further noting the Prosecution's submission that the United Nations Detention Unit cannot be expected to release the requested materials solely on the basis of a request from the Prosecution. Noting, however, that the Prosecution did not insist on the issuance of a subpoena, rather it was accepted that on order from the Chamber would suffice. Noting Rule 97 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which provides that "all communications between lawyer and client shall be regarded as privileged, and consequently not subject to disclosure at trial unless: (i) the client consents to such disclosure; or (ii) the client has voluntarily disclosed the content of the communication to a third party and the third party then gives evidence of that disclosure." Noting the general principle of proportionality, which states that: a measure in public international law is proportional only when suitable, necessary, and when its degree and scope remain in a reasonable relationship to the envisaged target; that procedural measures should never be capricious or excessive; and that it is sufficient to use a more lenient measure, it must be applied. Noting Rule 54 of the rules pursuant to which "a judge or a Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants, and transfer orders as may be necessary for the purposes of an investigate or for the preparation or conduct of the trial." Having heard the parties on this issue in Court on 3rd and 4th July, 2002. Noting that the Defence for Dr. Stakic does not object to that portion of the Prosecution's motion included in paragraph 2 in which it seeks an order to the United Nations Detention Unit to provide "original documents such as driver's license, passport, or similar documents that were in the possession of Milomir Stakic upon his arrival at the Detention Unit." Noting, however, that the Defence for Dr. Stakic argued in relation to the materials requested in paragraph 1 of the Prosecution's motion, that the subpoena is overbroad and overreaching and that such materials are protected by various privileges including the lawyer/client privilege. Noting further that in relation to this material, the Defence for Dr. Stakic argues that the Prosecution have failed to establish that issuance of such an order is necessary as is required under the rules. Noting that the parties have consented to the procedure set forth below, pursuant to which an ad litem judge of Trial Chamber II, not being a judge in this case, would review the requested materials before they are forwarded to the Prosecution. Considering that it is the opinion of the Chamber that, following the decision of the Trial Chamber in the case Prosecutor versus Zejnil Delalic et al, where it was held that an accused may not be compelled under the statute to provide a sample of his handwriting for the purpose of assisting the Prosecution in its investigation of the crimes charged against him, the accused, in not providing the Prosecution with a sample of his handwriting, has exercised his legitimate right to remain silent in these proceedings. Considering that, in order for the forensic handwriting examiner to carry out his assigned task of analyzing the signatures on the signed documents, he or she must necessarily have access to sufficiently large sample of Dr. Stakic's original handwriting and signatures. Considering that the Chamber is fully alive to the need to respect the lawyer/client privilege as set forth in Rule 97 of the Rules. Considering further that applying the principle of proportionality, especially in terms of necessity, and proportionality in its narrowest sense, the Trial Chamber finds that where in relation to any of the requested materials, it appears that the accused's right to privacy may be predominant, for example, letters to a medical practitioner, diaries, such material should be excluded pursuant to the procedure outlined below. Considering that the Registry of the Tribunal responsible for the management of the United Nations Detention Unit is a neutral organ, and therefore it cannot be expected to provide the requested materials solely on the basis of a request from the Prosecution. Considering, however, that a subpoena duces tecum seems not to be appropriate and necessary in these circumstances. Considering that on the basis of the foregoing that it is the opinion of the Trial Chamber that the provision of the requested materials are necessary for the conduct of the trial within the meaning of Rule 54 of the Rules and accordingly that the requested materials may be subject of on order of this Chamber. Pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules, hereby directs the United Nations Detention Unit to, first, identify any materials already within the possession of the United Nations Detention Unit (it is explicitly excluding material in Dr. Stakic's cell unit) comprising, one, original records or documents in the form of receipts, requests, and letters signed or handwritten by Milomir Stakic since his detention, other than communications between Dr. Stakic and any member of his Defence team; two, original documents such as driver's license, passport, or similar documents that were in the possession of Milomir Stakic upon his arrival at the Detention Unit. Second, to place these materials in a container which shall then be sealed and transferred to the premises of the International Tribunal (Chambers). And further request that the container be opened only in the presence of Judge Per Lindholm and counsel for Dr. Stakic who shall observe the following procedure: The appointed judge shall review the documents on the basis of the foregoing criteria (it is the lawyer/client privilege and proportionality) and exclude certain materials accordingly (the so-called excluded materials); second, at any time, the Stakic Defence may object to a document or any part thereof being included in the materials which are to be forwarded to the Prosecution (if necessary, portions of the documents may be severed); third, the appointed judge shall be the final arbiter (instead of the Chamber) for the purposes of this procedure of reviewing, undoubtedly leaving, however, all remedies available under these Rules untouched; four, at the end of this procedure, the excluded material shall be returned to the container, which shall be sealed and immediately returned to the premises of the United Nations Detention Unit. All the remaining documents shall be provided to the Prosecution in order to be forwarded to the appointed forensic handwriting examiner. I hope that this order can be and will be enforced forthwith, that as soon as possible, the "to be appointed" handwriting examiner has these samples in his hands. In reviewing the material, I saw that regarding List 4 of the OTP, List 4 of documents, there was a promise that would follow a new updated List 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have that available, but I would indicate it's not going to be the last list. If Your Honour wants to call the next one List 5, that's fine. But we have the list of documents that were signed, we believe, by Dr. Stakic that are not on the other lists, 1, 2, or 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just for the purposes to have an overview which further documents needs to be read out in open courtroom. And then we had one other document that should be translated. Do you remember we saw an interview on a videoclip, and it was done in English and B/C/S simultaneously, and also here it was promised that we would receive an interpretation of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does Your Honour mean the French translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, there was -- it's already now two weeks ago. We saw an interview in part in B/C/S and in part in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure which video that is. That was a video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not the one that we played Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no. It was another one. And I can probably have to come back to this, having then the correct exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's possible that it was -- I'm not sure I was even in Court when that was played, but it's possible it's the outtakes or it's part of the -- taken from the video that was played on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, it was a separate one. I have to come back to this. I thought it was self-evident which number this was. And finally, what about the still missing colour copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They are not back yet. It's in progress. Hopefully by tomorrow we will have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally from my point, you will receive today the scheduling order until December 13th. Hopefully we don't need all this time. But there you can see, of course, all the days needed until -- may be needed until 19th of September, and then leaving it open but taking care that on a provisional basis, the Courtroom II is available for this case until the end of this year. Anything else from your side? Nothing, nothing. Okay. Then let's turn to our witness of today. May I, whilst she is brought in, ask, she is a protected witness. Which kind of protection is the actual one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. She has a pseudonym and facial distortion. She has been granted those protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Shall we start in closed session for the name and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It would be appropriate, Your Honour, with your permission, if we could start in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In private session. I see no objection. The next pseudonym available is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Witness V, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness V already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you please be so kind and take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And may I, first of all, apologise that we are calling you here in the courtroom only "Witness." You may know it's for your personal protection only, that nobody hears your name and your name can't be read in our documents. And we start now in private session. That means, that nobody can hear what is said outside the courtroom. So please. You may start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be permitted to show this piece of paper which contains the name of the witness and get her to confirm that it is -- which could become an exhibit thereafter, and should be under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Could we have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit S188, marked confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S188, confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would take you to 1992, the month of April. Where were you in April in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went with my youngest son to my daughter Mediha because she had gotten married and had given birth to a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mediha residing at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Brkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near Bosanska Krupa, yes, the village of Brkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of April, you were staying with your daughter Mediha in Brkovica. During this time, or in early May, did you hear or get to know about the Serb takeover in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From my daughter Mediha's friend, I heard that there was a Serb takeover in Prijedor. I began to panic, and I tried to call my brothers who worked in the Celpak factory. I got through to my brother. I asked him how our mother was doing, whereupon he said that I should not wreck my nerves over her because she was all right. I began to panic and I wanted to go home, but I couldn't. I stayed for a month. There was no bus to take via Krupa or to go to Kljuc. After a month, I returned home Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with my youngest son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you panicked and called your brother who was working at Celpak. Now, you inquired about your mother. Did you inquire as to what was happening in the village of Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not supposed to, because I knew more or less what was happening, so that's why I was not in a position to ask. I just asked about our mother, and he said she was all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you call your brother once for the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't get through. I got through to a Serb man. Then I asked to speak to my brother, and he said: "He's not around." And I asked to speak to anyone from Carakovo. And he told me there were no people from Carakovo around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you called your brother who was working at the Celpak factory. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you returned after a month. Is it correct if I say that you returned to Carakovo on the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you called your brother for the second time, the person who answered the phone said that there was no one from Carakovo. Did you ask as to what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just said "thanks," and hung up. I didn't ask any questions. I saw many people from Krupa who had arrived there, and they told me that Krupa was in Serb hands and they told me what they did there. So I had some idea what was going on in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you returned to Carakovo with your youngest son. How old was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was, I think, 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness coming to Carakovo, you had lived there many, many years. Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born and I lived in Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the village well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. That's where I was born. That's where I was raised. My parents were born in Carakovo also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know approximately as to how many houses were there in Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between eight and nine hundred houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the majority of the ethnic group that was in Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, all Muslims. Five villages in a row all Muslims except for two Croatian house inside Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said five villages. Could you explain, tell the Chamber, as to what were these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zecovi, Carakovo, Hambarine, Rakovcani, Rizvanovici, Biscani, there were some other villages there, Sreca, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you returned to Carakovo, you lived with your family in the house, in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move around? Did you go to the Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day, I went to Prijedor. I couldn't go down the main road, the Sanski Most/Prijedor Road. We had to go through Gomjenica. And then for the first time, I saw a checkpoint in the village of Gomjenica. We were stopped there by Serb soldiers. They asked for our documents and asked what we were going to Prijedor for. We said we were going there to get some supplies. They said we shouldn't stay for longer than one hour, and then we had to return through the same checkpoint, which is what we did. We returned. They let us through the same checkpoint, and I returned home the same day. After eight days, I went to pick up my mother's pension. They told us to go to Tukovi. In Tukovi, I saw a tank, camouflaged in leaves, and the barrel was pointed towards Carakovo and Hambarine. We began to panic. We went to the post office. They didn't give us any money because they said the money was to be used for the Serb army, for fuel. Then we went back home. And from that day, every day, they came looking for something, fuel, vehicles, cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can I interrupt you and ask you a few more questions and clarify certain points. Now, you spoke about a checkpoint in Gomjenica. How far is Gomjenica from Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 2 kilometres probably, around 2 kilometres. Over the Sana, there's a bridge to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke about another checkpoint in Tukovi where you saw a tank. Now, how far was this checkpoint from Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a kilometre and a half, because between Prijedor and Carakovo, there are 2 kilometres, maybe a kilometre and a half. That's where the tank was parked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was on the Sanski Most/Prijedor main road. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's next to the River Sana. On the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke about people in uniforms. Did you recognise what uniforms, what were the uniforms? Could you explain, describe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, camouflage uniforms. I also recognised the people who were manning the checkpoints in Carakovo, the Sanski Road, the road to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any names of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that checkpoint next to the tank, Drago Tintar and Mico Jurusic were standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they from the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drago Tintar was from Tukovi, and I think Jurusic lived somewhere in Prijedor. But I knew him from the Carakovo/Prijedor bus line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, talking about this checkpoint, were the people able to move freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really freely, because they stopped people there. They asked questions about what you were going to Prijedor for. It was no longer yours. It was in Serb hands. You have no business there. You didn't want to go to war with us. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get your food and any other essentials from the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was quite difficult. In June, we could, but in July, no longer, because as soon as you were recognised, identified as a Muslim, you could no longer buy anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you spoke about two checkpoints, one in Gomjenica and the other one in Tukovi. Did you see another checkpoint in some other place, in the outskirts of Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I was on my way back from Brkovica to Carakovo, in May, when I was going back home, I saw a checkpoint up there in Sanski Most. Soldiers were stopping trucks, searching them, and then letting them through from Sanski Most on the road to Prijedor. That was the first time I saw this checkpoint apart from the two other ones I had seen before. Soldiers wearing uniforms, all Serb soldiers. I couldn't see a Muslim anywhere around. So I began to panic. I didn't know what would happen to me. But they didn't do anything to me. They just looked at my ID. They said: "Oh you're from Prijedor" and then they let me through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I will take your mind to another area. After the Serb takeover in April 1992, the following months, did you listen to the broadcast in the Radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They cut off electricity, so we had no electricity, but some people still listened to the radio, rode around on their bikes. We listened to the news. We heard about Mirza Mujadzic and Hilmija Hopovac. Mostly, there were requests to surrender. I did not really know those people. Day in, day out, they called for them to surrender. They called for weapons to be turned in, the hunting rifles that people had. They had already turned those weapons in. They turned these -- those weapons in at the place where weapons were being collected, but they still asked for more weapons to be turned in. They began to panic, and people started to run to the woods. In the evening, Serbs would enter the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can I interrupt you there. I will go step by step. I need to clarify certain points. Now, you mentioned the name of Hilmija Hopovac and Mirza Mujadzic. You said that you don't know these people, but do you know as to what position they held and what they did during that time and as to why there was a call to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that they had founded the SDA, the party. I can't say whether that was true or not, but that's what they called them for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that whether this Hilmija Hopovac or Mirza Mujadzic held any position in the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said there was a call to surrender weapons. Did anybody from your village surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were people who had hunting rifles, and they took these hunting rifles. And I mean they had pistols as well, and they had permits and they handed all that in. They handed all that in by the village road, yes, as far as I could hear. I don't know. I didn't have any such thing. I had nothing to hand in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you didn't have a weapon, but did you know that the others handed over the hunting rifles that they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did. Yes. They handed them in. My neighbours, as far as I know, those who had rifles, they took them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the month of June in 1992, you spent your time in the village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Serb soldiers come to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, every day, they came into the village, and they asked for something. Fuel, cars, or whatever we had, cattle, animals, they would slaughter them, and they would eat. They were also looking for people. For example, the women knew what was going on, and some of them would say: "Well, my man is working in Austria, my man is working Slovenia." But at any rate, only if they knew, because they were neighbours, that these people were actually there, they would mistreat the women, they could curse them. They would say: "We know they are there, they are hiding," things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the Serb soldiers who came during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Dragan Tintar and Mico Jurusic for the most part. And then there were some other people there, younger ones, older ones, I don't know. But I recognised them because with Dragan Tintar -- I mean, I knew him. He would come to (redacted) We would talk. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they dressed in uniform? Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were carrying rifles, those automatic rifles. And uniforms, and Drago, once, I saw actually when he came to pick up a neighbour of mine --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, may I interrupt you. And please, answer my questions. Now, during the month of June in 1992, did any people from the other villages come to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People fled from Hambarine, from the village of Hambarine, to our village because the Serbs had already taken over their village, and then they fled. Some went to Rizvanovici, some to Carakovo, so some were staying at our village, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people from Hambarine, were they children and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Women, children, old people, people who were sickly. Whoever could escape, escaped. And those who could not stayed, and some of them they caught and took to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to these people who came from the other villages such as Hambarine, did they tell you that the men were arrested and taken away to the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They talked. The young people, whoever they got at home or in the fields or in the woods, wherever, whoever managed to escape escaped to our village. And that's how they got there, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they said that the Serbs had already taken over their village. Did they say what the Serbs did in their village? What did they mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this after the attack on the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the attack happened, yes, that's when the women fled. They started shelling Carakovo and Hambarine the same day. And that day, they barged into Hambarine, and then the women fled from there. Actually, they stayed in the village of Hambarine, they did. And then a month later, they also attacked Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will come to that. Now, how long did the people from Hambarine stay in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A month. We were together until Carakovo fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the 23rd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the day that the Serbs attack the village of Carakovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a terrible day, a sad day. I remember that day. At 9.00 in the morning, I went to my neighbour's home to bring some food because his children were staying with me. That is 2 kilometres down the road from my place. This neighbour said that there is an attack that is going to be launched against Carakovo. He heard the tanks coming. And I said: "I'm going home. The children are there. And my mother is there, and the women who were staying with me." I didn't even manage to get to my house. They were already --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have interrupted you. But I would like to know the name of your neighbour who came and said that the village is being attacked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name is Adem Hopovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Adem Hopovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was Adem Hopovac's house from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he came, and he was not in the house when you went to his house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He slept somewhere, at his sister's in Carakovo actually. And then when I managed to get some food from him, he managed to get there, too. And then he did notice these tanks moving towards Carakovo. And then he said: "The army is coming. What are we going to do"? And I said to him, Adem, I'm going home. Our children are on their own. And a lady friend was with me, and her son, and a neighbour. And then behind Adem's house, there was some corn, and then we started running through these corn fields taking a shortcut in order to get home as soon as possible. There was shooting, and there was this thunder coming from the tanks. What could I do? I couldn't even reach my home. And then through the woods, we moved to the school, and then the soldiers stopped there, and they were holding rifles. And then this young man who was behind me, this colleague of mine who was with me, he noticed them. I managed to get out of the woods about a metre, and then he grabbed me by the shoulders, and pulled me back. And then we went back through these woods and through the corn fields, and there were 15 or 20 dulums of corn. It was a big field. And then we stayed there until about 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- interrupt, please, at page 18, line 25, may the location be redacted please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Plead proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were hiding in the corn field which was between the woods, did you see the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them, but I did hear the shooting, and I heard the tanks, and I heard the screams of women and children. I heard them crying. And then I saw houses that were burning straight away. We were still in the corn fields. We thought it would stop. But then, no, the screaming was going on, and they were shouting. And they were going through the woods as if it were some kind of a hunt. When Mujo Hopovac's house was on fire, we got up, and we tried to go back to Adem's house to move towards it by the house of Danica. They are neighbours. And then the shooting abated a bit. As we approached the house, Danica's house, we found her house. He said that they had searched the house, and that they told him not to go anywhere, that they would be coming back. As for Adem Hopovac's house, and his son's house, everything was taken out, everything that they had. The washing machine, the VCR, everything that they had, and when I came, I saw them loading vehicles. Some were going towards Rastovci and others towards Prijedor. We hid there. I asked Danica's husband to give me a cigarette so that I could light up. I saw women going, and I saw women ringing their hands in dismay and saying that they burned their sheds. And then Husein Sijacic's wife was there, and -- oh, I've forgotten the name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Jasmin, Jasmin Sijacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Jasmin. Their wives and children went towards Prijedor, and their men were killed behind the houses. Then we set out slowly. The shooting abated and everything else. And then we started moving towards my house. When I came to my house --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before you go to your house, may I interrupt you. I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any warning from the Serbs before the attack to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were issuing these warnings about weapons, weapons should be handed in. Every day, day in and day out, they were saying that weapons should be handed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. Before the attack, before the tanks came into the town, they never gave you a warning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were threatening people that they would have to be mobilised and that they had to report for mobilisation. They were calling them day in, day out. But our people did not dare respond. They didn't want to go and fight in Croatia. They were threatening Mujadzic and Hopovac. They were actually using their very own last names. They said: "Whoever had the last name of Mujadzic and Hopovac, that they would kill these families." But we didn't pay attention to that because we thought that that wouldn't really happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said you heard the wife of Husein Sijacic and Jasmin Sijacic saying that their men were killed. Did you hear or see any other men being taken into custody and being taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw people as they were leaving en mass. Men, women, and children going on buses. They were being taken somewhere, but I didn't know where they were being taken?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know a person by the name of Rubija Redzic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this woman was killed right in front of her own house on that day. On that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, explain as to what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rubija Redzic was lying dead in front of her house. The Serbs had killed her on that day. I was passing by there from Adem Hopovac's house. I was passing in front of Rubija's house as I was going to y house. I saw her dead. After that, I heard that the Serbs had come there and that they killed her in front of her house. The woman didn't manage to escape. She didn't manage to hide anywhere, so she was lying in front of her own house dead. Fehim also, killed right in front of her house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll get to that. We'll go step by step slowly. Did you see any injuries on Rubija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was lying on the stomach, and she was bloody up here, here I saw her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You showed the place. Was it the head that you saw blood or injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the head, up here, that's where the blood was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was Rubija? Was she a villager? Was she staying in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she was a local villager. She lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about a person by the name of Fehim. Is it Fehim Karupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karupovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was also born there in the village. First of all, I saw Adem Hopovac there. Adem was killed, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will come to that. What did you see? Where did you see Fehim and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fehim was lying on his back in front of his own house. He had been shot in the chest, and in the hands -- he was lying like this. So there were bullet holes in his chest, on his hands, and also in the forehead, and he was lying on the back like that in front of his own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was -- you saw him dead in front of his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he was also a Muslim from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's a Muslim, too, yes. He was born there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how old were Fehim and Rubija, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rubija was born in 1937 because I talked to her children. And Fehim was born in 1940.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you also saw Adem Hopovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Adem was lying by his house on the stomach. Again, he was wounded in the back, and his legs were spread out like this because I was -- this was the first time I saw a dead man, I was frightened. I panicked, and then from there, we went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any injuries on Adem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the back, a bullet had hit him in the back. He was lying on the stomach, and a bullet had gone through his shirt and his legs were spread out and his head was a bit slanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Adem, how old was he, and what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim, about 60 years old. He was a retiree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you saw Adem Hopovac dead, and his body, you proceeded to go to your house. Did you come to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then I came to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct if I say Adem's son was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Adem's son was at my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was 25 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell Adem's son as to what had happened to his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I told him. When he saw me, he started crying. He said: "Are you alive?" And I said, "Yes." I said, "Son, unfortunately your father got killed." And his mother was in the village of Zecovi, and he said, "Would you please be so good as to go with me to my mother's to tell her that my father got killed." And then we went to Zecovi. We arrived in Zecovi. His mother was a heart patient. She was happy when she saw him. She said, "Son, why have you come? Are you hungry?" And then she found a piece of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give the information to the wife of Adem that Adem was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't tell her directly, but we told the woman at whose place she was staying. We said: "Hata, take care of Adem's wife. Adem was killed." Since Adem's wife was sick, and this other person with whom she was saying was an old woman, we said, "Try to get over to my place, to Carakovo." And I and Adem's son left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you come to that, how far was Zecovi from Carakovo, from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A kilometre, a kilometre between the village of Carakovo and the village of Zecovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, after you gave the information to Hata and Adem's wife about the death of Adem, then you returned to come to your house in Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Until 10.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on your way from Hata's house which is in Zecovi, did you pass a place which you call the Bare, or which is in English the swamp, swamp area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But grass is also cut there, too, but yes, we call the place bare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this place, did you see any person's killed, or dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I came across eight dead bodies. I can't remember all of them now. They were lying there. I passed by. I recognised Asim Redzic, and then I panicked. I went home to my brother's, and I said to my brothers: "There are many dead people lying in "Bare". Asim is among them. Perhaps the rest are not from our villages." And then my brothers and I went there. We recognised all the people who were there, Hopovac, Huse, Suad, his young son; Malovcic, Fadil, his cousin, also a young man. Then Velid Hopovac, Nijaz, his brother; Redzic Asim, Redzic Nijaz, I think his first name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will come to these people, the names of these people a little later. Now, did you see the body of Asim Redzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the injuries that he had sustained or suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was also wounded in the head. He was lying on the back. When I approached him nearby, when we had returned, I saw that his shirt was bullet-riddled, and that he had many wounds in the chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about another person by the name of Nijaz Redzic. He was also a person who was dead and where you saw the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Asim Redzic and Nijaz Redzic, how old were they approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim was 60, almost 61. And Nijaz was a youngish man, about 38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke about a person by the name of Huse Hopovac and his son Suad. Am I correct, you saw their bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Huse Hopovac, how old was he and his son Suad? If you know approximately, what was their age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Huse was born in 1940. And the young boy Suad was born in 1974. He went to school with my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned another name by the name of Fadil Malovcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Malovcic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you saw dead was his nephew. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Malovcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the first name? It's all right. We will move on. Then you also spoke about a person by the name of Nijaz Hopovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other person was his brother. Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his brother, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he Mirhad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirhad, yes. Mirhad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they young people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Youngish people. I think Nijaz Hopovac was perhaps born in 1955, and his brother was about three years younger than him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fadil Malovcic and his nephew, how old was his nephew, if you know approximately? Was he a young boy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Born in 1974. He also went to school with my daughter. Fadil, I think, was born in 1961. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when these bodies were brought by your brothers, were the Serbs still around, the Serb soldiers? Did you hear the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day, every hour, they were there. But when it got dark, they took a horse cart, and then they went through the woods to Asim Redzic's house, because there is a cemetery there. And the others had stayed behind in order to dig the graves because if you would be digging in the field, then they would see you and shoot at you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you buried all these people, the dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you later hear from a person by the name of Husein Malovcic as to what happened to these people whom you found dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to Travnik, Husein also went with us. One day, we went out in front of the barracks, and we were sitting there and he was crying. And he was saying: "All our children are gone. Military men came in uniforms." He recognised some of them. Vasiljevic was his last name. I don't know his first name. And then he said to Husein that they would only take them for interrogation. Then they would return them home. And then his son Fadil was even barefoot at the time, and he wanted to go back to put his shoes on. And then he said: "Come on, Fadil." Because they were colleagues. They knew each other. He said: "You won't need that." And then they took them through the woods behind the house. About 300 metres behind Husein's house, there is a forest. And then they started beating them there with their hands and pushing them. Nijaz's brother was lame, and he couldn't walk properly. And then every time the soldier would hit him, he would fall. And then to "bare" you had to walk for about an hour, and that is where their lives came to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Husein Malovcic was the father of Fadil Malovcic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the next two days after the 23rd of July, 1992, did you see Serbs come into your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw them every single day, every hour. In the evening, we couldn't sleep in our houses. They requested that we keep the lights on, but there was no electricity, so that they could tell that there were people inside the houses. They would come to the houses in the evening, take people off, kill and maltreat them. We hid in the woods. We couldn't even stay in our houses. Early in the morning, we would get back to our house, make some food for ourselves, and they would shoot again. We saw them walk by with rifles, sometimes on horse-drawn carts. Sometimes they walked. Sometimes they used armed personnel carriers, things like that. Until eventually we were removed from Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now, when you saw this during these days, did the Serb soldiers come and take away anything from your house or from your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came one day to my sister's place looking for a car. She gave them gold. They were looking for a tractor, for a scythe. All the mechanic tools, they took everything. They came back in the evening and killed everyone in the house. I didn't see him, but I spoke to my son-in-law. There was blood on his hands. He was crying. My grandfather was behind the door. He had a heart attack. They cut up his body. The next house was perhaps 200 metres away. Over a hundred women and children slept in my house then. Elderly people, too. You had to keep your head down all the time because there were bullets flying all over the place between the two houses. In the morning, I could no longer take it so I went to the other house where they were staying. I found my brother's colleague at the checkpoint. I said: "Good afternoon."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry to have interrupted you. Before you go to that area, I need to ask you some questions with regard to certain other areas. We will come to that later. Now, we were talking about the two days after -- that is 25th or 26th of July. Now, you say that the Serb soldiers used to come to your village and take away things. Did they take a tractor from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister's tractor, that's the one they took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take money from your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They took money and gold, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all wearing uniforms, soldiers, civilians, you couldn't tell because they all wore the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recall a person by the name of Besim Music whom you took to the hospital during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 223rd, he was outside his own house. He was shredding corn when Serb soldiers came. They put him in a car and took him off somewhere. They beat him in the car. They broke his bones and threw him out perhaps 30 metres down the road further from the house. They threw him out there. He moaned and groaned, and you could hear his moans in the woods where our people were staying. They brought him in a horse cart up there where he could be helped. He spent a day or two with us. We dressed his wounds. His body was swollen. They shot him not directly in the head, but through the head, and then his skin was ripped. His legs were also like that, his arms. We could no longer continue like that. My brothers asked me for him to be taken to a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you took him to the hospital on the 25th of July, 1992, in a horse cart. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Which hospital did you take him to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a hospital in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to his wife, Badema? Did you see her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see her. But the woman neighbour who buried her son at her place saw her. She had been taken away. She had been verbally abused and told to show them where the hideouts used by the Green Berets were. She yelled and cried and said she didn't know where that was. They took her to the woods where they killed her and Ramiz Rekic [phoen]. They killed them together. Ramiz was buried by his father and mother and Badema's body remained lying outside because there was no one to bury her. No one was able to, so she wasn't buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this time, did you know persons by the name of Ermin Sijacic and Huse Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw their bodies, their dead bodies. When they were brought to the cemetery near my house, Nermin Sijacic's father found their bodies in a field. They dug their graves and brought their bodies there in wheelbarrows. They were cut up across their chests. Their faces were disfigured. There was blood on their skin, and their faces were bullet-pimpled. We buried them there in Mezaluci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was after the attack on the 23rd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 24rd, we buried them. His father came from the woods and saw them lying, their dead bodies, in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient time to have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before the break, we were talking about you seeing the bodies of Huse Salihovic and Ermin Sijacic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time, did you see the body of Nasif Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see the body, but I saw his son burying him. There was blood on his hands. I talked to him, and he said he found him in the house in the kitchen behind the door. He was all cut up by bullets, and then he buried him in his garden outside the house. The body had been looked at by the national committee, and they had seen it and studied it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Nasif Dizdarevic was then living in Zecovi. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I say you saw the body of Nasif Dizdarevic when it was buried, am I correct that it was on the 27th of July, 1992? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on the 27th of July, 1992, when you saw Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, talking about these days in July 1992, after the attack on your village, Carakovo, were there people staying in your house taking refuge in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from Hambarine, from Zecovi, from all over the place, they came to my house. Sometimes we slept in the house, but more often, we slept in the woods because Serb soldiers would come to the house every night. If they found anyone inside the house, they would kill them. Wherever they found families in the village of Zecovi, they killed them. We were seized by panic and we started to run and hide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 28th of July, 1992, did you and two others go to the centre of the town in Carakovo and speak to any of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I came across a colleague of my brothers who worked with them in the Celpak factory. He was also wearing a uniform and carrying a rifle. He recognised me. I said, "Good afternoon. I came here to ask you what we should do, because I can no longer stay at my house with the other people who were staying in my house." And he said, "We are here --" that was a Wednesday, until Saturday. "We guarantee that you stay, and then afterwards, the army from Serbia would be here, and I can give you no further guarantees. Something had to be done." I returned home. I told the people who were staying there what I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had been told. I no longer want to stay here. What do I need this house for in this situation? I'm going over there to surrender. And then the other neighbours who were staying in their own houses, started out with us, with me, and they said we should carry a white flag and assemble there with the other people. Around a hundred people started out from my house, and there were more people on the way to this home, building. They kept us there for three hours. They maltreated us. "Where are you going to? Who are you going to? Here's your Alija now. You wanted your own state. Go home." And we just kept silent, kept our heads down. They didn't even give us water or food. Some old men took the water from the horses to give to the children to drink, but they wouldn't let them. And next to us, a friend from a neighbouring village sat there. She had buried her two sons and a number of neighbours. She sat in front of us with two small children. Her husband had been killed. A Serb came over and said, "Okay, start making your beds." And then she moaned, and then my relative by the name of (redacted) came up to him and said, "Look my son, I'll make the bed. Leave this woman alone." He started to curse her, the Serb. And then another patrol came, and they said, "Come on, let's go. We've got the buses here for you".

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: There was a reference, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the name on line 15 please be redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now, to clarify certain points, you, with the other people who were in your house and in the village with a white flag came to the centre of Carakovo, which is called the dom. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is where you were explaining as to what the soldiers told you and how they conducted themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the majority of the people who were there, were almost the people the children, the women, and the old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, elderly people, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before this, the military-aged people, the young men were taken into custody and taken away. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some had been taken away, and some were not allowed to come there and surrender. They just hid in the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you stayed there for a couple of hours in the dom, in the centre of the town, were you all asked to go to another place by the name of Zegar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the maltreatment and after being detained for several hours, armed soldiers took us to -- escorted us to Zegar, and the buses came there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you explain what this place you call Zegar is. Is it a name of a place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a part of Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a bridge which is called the Zegar Bridge, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Zegar bridge. Just near the bridge, that's where we were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were taken, escorted by -- was it the Serb soldiers who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they took us there. We went two by two, looking in front, because we couldn't look anywhere else. We were not allowed. Every 2 metres there was a Serb soldier with a rifle standing facing us. And they escorted us all the way to Zegar like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Zegar from the centre of Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in Carakovo actually. It's a kilometre from the dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a kilometre from the dom to Zegar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When you were taken to the place called the Zegar, did you see a group of young men who had been brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you observe? How did they look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group of Muslims who were stopped there, they were stripped bare to their waist. They were told to put their hands behind their back, and they were just standing there. They were just stopped. I didn't know what was going on, why they were kept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any things lying on the ground where this group was standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, their clothes. Jackets, shirts, IDs, it was all lying on the ground. But we were not allowed to pick any of those items up. So when we came to the house, there were soldiers looking from the windows so that -- making sure no one would pick up any of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this moment, did buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the buses began to arrive, and people were loaded into these buses. They just loaded up to 150 people on to one bus, women, children, as many as they could fit inside a bus. Five buses one after the other, and I was in the last bus with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these buses from Autotransport Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were driving the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb soldiers did. I don't know, because I didn't recognise any of them then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you got into the bus, when you were about to get into the bus, did you see a person by the name of Hasib Simbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He came with us. He was my neighbour. He came with us to the dom, to Zegar. He stood behind me. I entered. And then he put his foot on the first step of the bus, and his coat fell off. But among all those soldiers, Drago Tintar came, grabbed him, and asked him, "Where are you going to Hasib? You can't go. You're not allowed to leave." The bus was still there, and he grabbed him and pushed him, made him walk in front of him towards the bridge. Not even 3 metres away. He took out his gun from the belt. He shot Hasib, and Hasib fell down, and then the bus left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He shot him here, and then he fell down on his back, right in his forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Tintar was a Serb soldier. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he dressed in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he from Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you boarded the bus, where were you all taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Trnopolje. That's where we found...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I stopped you. Before we speak about -- talk about Trnopolje, could I ask you another question. Did you -- you said that Tintar was dressed in a uniform. What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform, just the usual camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, going back to the trip to Trnopolje, you all were taken to Trnopolje the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some people had stayed behind, people who didn't leave on the same day. But those five buses went to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just spent the night there. And then headed off for Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was some sort of a centre, a school building. I didn't know Trnopolje very well. They hoarded us in there. There were people sleeping outside also. There was a wire fence. Bread was to be paid for, but was not given to us on the same day. So we just spent the night there, some without a roof over their heads and some inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after that night in Trnopolje, were you all transferred to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came. They said the trucks would be there, and then "You will go to your own country." A Serb came over and told us. Some came and said, "There is no fuel. We must put some money together to get fuel." But at a certain point, we heard a truck coming. They told us to go to a room and hoarded us into a room. As many people as could fit inside, and even more. They kicked us and pushed us. Two buses and three trucks came, and we stayed there. They said, "You'll spend the night here. There's no more transport today." After 20 minutes, another truck came, and then those of us who were in the other hall, they hoarded us on to that bus, and then we left. Trucks were covered with ground sheets, so you couldn't tell where you were going. You didn't know where you were being taken to. They stopped us in two different places. Children were asking for water, of course. We were followed by two cars. I don't know what those cars were, to give us water. And then soldiers were going around with bags to collect money and gold. If you had none, he would slap the child and hold a bayonet up to the child's head. And whoever had some money or gold had to give it to them. We were stopped like that twice and maltreated. And then we reached Vlasic. We got out of the bus there. They made us walk for about 500 metres. I was afraid. It was dark already, around 9.00 in the evening. I saw them standing there by the road side with beards all wearing uniforms. And they said, "Here you are, this is your country. That's what you've asked for." There was our own army and our own uniforms waiting there for us, and they took us to the barracks in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence is prepared to commence the cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. V. I will speak to you like this. As Judge Schomburg has already spoken to you for your own personal protection. We speak the same language, so there can be problems. When you answer, you should try to pause a little after my question so there's no overlap between question and answer. That's for the sake of the interpretation service. Mrs. V, how many times were you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, can we go to private session. I have to mention some names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, today when I put some questions to you, I will refer to certain pages and certain lines in your statements, but that should not confuse you. That is simply for the transcript so that the Honourable Judges could follow what we are talking about. In your statement dated 2000, the B/C/S version is page 2, paragraph 3, and the English version is page 2, paragraph 3, you say the following: "Around the 4th or 5th of May, Prijedor fell. I was in Brkovica visiting one of my daughters at the time. My youngest son was also with me. My other two children were in Carakovo at this time with my mother. I was able to talk to my brother on one occasion who told me that things were okay in Carakovo." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your brother give you any more details concerning the situation as it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask either because this was on the telephone after all, and I just asked him how mother was doing. And he said, don't worry, mother is fine. And we both knew what it was all about, because I had heard from people who had come to Brkovica from Krupa what had happened to Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you reached Carakovo, was the situation still okay in Carakovo, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite tense. People were not working. They were afraid of mobilisation, what they should do, what they should respond to. They didn't want to go and kill anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any armed conflicts at the time in Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did the local population organise village patrols or night patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were night patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated 2000, the B/C/S version page 2, paragraph 4, and the English version, page 2, paragraph 4, you say the following: "On the 7th of May, my son-in-law went to Bihac, and he heard there was a bus to Prijedor by way of Banja Luka or Kljuc."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "So he suggested I go via Kljuc because he thought it was safer."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That means that bus lines were operating at the time. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there weren't. They were stopped, and then they let one line operate to Kljuc and Banja Luka. I decided to go to Kljuc. But there was no bus from Prijedor to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many passengers were on the bus? Can you remember? Was the bus full, empty, half full?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sort of, not many people were going to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the bus ticket was customary or was it more expensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was more expensive. My son-in-law had to lend me some money because I didn't have enough to pay for the bus ticket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When entering the bus, did anybody ask you for a permit or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My ID, and that is when I took the bus from Kljuc to Prijedor. Actually they asked in Sanski Most for my ID. Milim Birt [phoen] I think was the name of the place in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was everybody asked to show their IDs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm referring to your statement dated 2000, the B/C/S version, page 2, paragraph 5, and the English version, page 2, paragraph 5, line 3, you say the following: "At this time, the Serbs were looking for men from my village to mobilise to fight in the war in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "On one occasion, our young men were mobilised into the reserve."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this refer to the period before or after the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before, before. I think it was already in April that my brothers were mobilised. They left home, went for three days, and then came back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not manage to interpret the last sentence you said. I'm just going to read to you what is in the transcript. You said that your brothers had left home. They went for three days, and then came back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you say something after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not respond to mobilisation call-ups any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how mobilisation was carried out? Were call-up papers sent that people were supposed to respond to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time they responded, they received call-up papers. The second time they called them, they called them via Radio Prijedor, and then everybody was supposed to report for mobilisation. But they did not respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your statement from the year 2000, B/C/S version is page 2, paragraph 2, line 2, the English version, page 2, paragraph 2, you say the following: "In 1990, I began to notice people in my area talk about war." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, yes, I worked (redacted), and a friend, his name was -- I've forgotten his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
