utterances.text: It is open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far away your village was from the centre of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was exactly 9 kilometres to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the road to Prijedor, through which villages did you pass, or rather, what ethnicity were the people in the villages that you passed through on your way to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I get out of my village, all of it is Muslim population. I mean, there were -- I mean, up to Tukovi, there were no Serbs, and then in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Tukovi, it was a mixed population both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement from the year 2000, B/C/S version page 3, paragraph 2, the English version page 3, paragraph 1, you talk about checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say the following: "I saw all three checkpoints from close quarters. I was able to see the first and second checkpoints whenever I went to the town of Prijedor. The third one I could not see from my house, but on numerous occasions, I passed close to it." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw. I saw these checkpoints when I passed by them when I went to Prijedor and when I went back from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how often you went to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on the third or fourth day, when necessary. For example, when a neighbour would come and say something was needed. I don't know. I mean, I really did not doubt these Serbs. And I had the courage to go to buy things that they would let us buy. And what they didn't let us, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you can say that you went every three or four days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the checking at the checkpoints, did you move about unhindered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would explain to us that we should not stay in Prijedor, that we would have to go back within an hour. And then really quickly, you would go and buy whatever you needed, and then go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to go to Prijedor, did you need a special permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, they didn't ask for any such thing. Later on, they wouldn't let anyone pass the checkpoint without a permit. You had to go to the MUP to get a permit. A lady neighbour of mine, her man was in the Serb army, and then he got me one of these permits, and I went to Prijedor only once that way. I didn't go more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say the beginning, they didn't ask for these permits. For how long was it not necessary to have these permits? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, my God, it was about ten days. After that, they asked for permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you go to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you sometimes travel by car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Once, we set off in a horse cart. They let us go in Zegar. But down there, by the Prijedor bridge, they mistreated us. They wanted to take us -- to send us back. But then somebody else came, I don't know, somebody with some kind of insignia. They said, "Let the people go." And then people who had money said that we had to take their Serb and we changed this in the bank. I mean, those who had those dinars, they had to change it for this I don't know what. I can't remember the name. So people who had money, they had to exchange the money. We bought what we needed and...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did money change at that time? Could you please explain this to us a bit. What kind of Serb money was this at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how to explain this to you. It was some kind of billions. I know that it was Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the bank note it said "Banja Luka"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Yugoslav dinars were not being used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were being used, too, but for the most part, we had to take their money. I had nothing to change, so I didn't take it. But others who had more money, they needed it, and then they exchanged their money.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from going to Prijedor, did you go anywhere else in May 1992, and also in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, except for Prijedor and the village, my village where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one day I went there with a friend. She was from Ljubija. She went to see her mother there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did it happen that you and the other people from your village decided to take shelter in your house precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because my house was about 2 kilometres from the asphalt road. And they take over to my place and asked me whether I could stay there, as my house was slightly bigger, 12 or 16. So more people could fit inside. So we decided to stay there. But as I've told you, perhaps we spent two or three nights there, and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained to us today and you mentioned in your statement that your village was attacked on the 23rd of June -- 23rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is your village near the Kurevo woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not far from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there armed people in your village just prior to the conflict, to the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any armed people in the Kurevo woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that either. I didn't see anyone, and I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from other people that there were armed groups in the Kurevo woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those days, I was struggling to be alive with my -- to stay alive with my children and my mother. My mother was born in 1920. We just fled out of fear. I didn't want to know who was armed and who wasn't. I just wanted them not to touch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the first person who told you, as you say in your statement dated 2001, B/C/S page 3, paragraph 1, English statement, page 2, paragraph 6, that "in the Kurevo woods, there were armed Green Berets."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it on the radio. The Serb army, for the people in Kurevo, the Green Berets, to surrender. That was over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated 2000, B/C/S version, page 4, paragraph 4, English version also page 4, paragraph 4, you say that you heard that 5.000 Serb soldiers were in your village during the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's indeed what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also say that they were all masked to prevent you from identifying them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it in Travnik when I got there because people kept arriving from Kljuc. They were returning and shouting, they were shouting: "The village was dangerous. And we had no problems in that village. We expelled them all and killed them all without a problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see these masked soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see when I ran from the corn field towards a house outside the school building, I saw masked soldiers wearing rifles, and I heard cries and yells. And I couldn't see anything more than that from the corn field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Aside from wearing camouflage uniforms, were they masked in any other way to be so difficult to identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My neighbours said that they also applied masks all over their bodies. Husein recognised the one who had taken the people from his house. He recognised another one who had his face painted. He recognised him by his voice because he had come to see him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you hear this from Husein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Travnik, when we met in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated 2000, and you've also mentioned this today in Court, B/C/S version, bottom of page 5, English version, page 5, paragraph 3 -- paragraph 5, you describe what took place on the 25th of July, 1992 when you took Besic Music and another man by the name of Ramo from Hambarine whom you met at the first checkpoint, you say that you took them to the hospital in Prijedor. And then returned to Carakovo. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you take these two persons to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first went to ask the patrol at the checkpoint. I said I had some people with me who were wounded, whether I could take them to the hospital. They said that I could, but that I also had to take Ramo. That was perhaps half a kilometre from there. They put Besim on a horse cart. I never used a horse cart before, so I didn't quite know what to do. I came up to Ramo, his wife was there, too. His arm was out of joint, and he was sitting there with his wife. He sat on the horse cart with his wife, and then at the checkpoint, when I came there with the horses down in Zegar, they didn't do anything there. A soldier walked up to me wearing a uniform. "Where are you headed to with these people? Oh, come on, you shot at us from the woods. Now you see these people are wounded." He was still conscious. He said: "My wife didn't do anything. I didn't do anything either. They beat me up in my own home. They put them on a horse cart, and several hundred metres down the road they shot people through the head. They threw him out." He was wounded. I don't know how he was wounded I didn't talk to them. I took them to the hospital. That's as far as I got. I went inside. There was a doctor and a lady doctor standing there. "Good afternoon. Good afternoon. I brought these people to you. They are wounded. What are their names?" I said, "Besim Music. And Ramo. I didn't know his last name." And the lady doctor told me, "Oh, that's the one." I didn't show what she was talking about. They were looking for a man named Besim Music who was supposedly a leader of the SDA. That was another man. And the doctors examined him, and then the doctor said his blood pressure is high. He's about to have a heart attack. We said nothing, and he said they would keep him at the hospital, but no visits allowed. Once we were out of the hospital, myself and my sister who was driving with me, a man came out in a black uniform with a handbag and shirt, and he said, "Are you the one who brought these wounded people here?" I said "Yes." He said, "Don't even budge from here until I'm back." And then he told me, "You're free to go. You can thank God that this is not the Besim we were looking for because we wouldn't just let you go." I said -- sat on the horse cart, and my cousin said, "Let's get something for the children." And then another soldier came running out holding a rifle. He said, "Fuck your Muslim mother. What are you sniffing around here for?" I ran off, and my sister stayed there. I went 500 metres down the road, and then waited for her. I said, "Sister, what had happened?" And she said, "There's our woman with the horses there." And she pulled him against her chest. And he said, "Don't touch this woman." I ran over there and sat on the cart, and then we left, reached the checkpoint at Carakovo on the way into Zegar. They stopped us and asked us what we had taken there. I saw Drago Tintar sitting over there at a table, and he shouted over at them "Let them go." And then I returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us today that following the attack, electricity was cut in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, even before the attack, we didn't have any electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us if electricity supply was irregular or there was none at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since when was the electricity supply cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came from Brkovica in May, there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they have electricity in Prijedor? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In Prijedor, it was clear for all to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You could see it all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb villages have electricity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because across the water, across the river, the River Sana, you could see the Serb villages, and they did have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Except for the fact that every three or four days you could go to Prijedor, did you -- were you able to produce food yourself? Did you have a garden or a field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not much. They gave us fuel to reap, but we didn't eat a single corn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you speak about negotiations with the soldier at the checkpoint, the checkpoint you went to with the two other women, Jasminka and Fatija Karupovic, how did this happen? Who provided the initiative for you to go there and talk there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our own initiative. I had no more courage to stay at home, no food and no electricity. Every day, you're just waiting to be killed. So I decided myself to go there, and I asked them whether they would come with me. But I met a colleague there, a man was standing there they checkpoint. He said, "Good afternoon." "Good afternoon." He was ashamed to be there, but he said, "We have no choice. We have to be here."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone else next to him at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, further down. He was talking to me. The dom, the local commune, it was all Serb army. They were shooting, and I didn't know what was happening because you couldn't see anything there. Our people whom they caught in the woods, they brought them here to kill them. It was only later when I got to Travnik that I found out what had been happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone attack you or wound you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone wounded or killed at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did the soldier say? Who authorised him to negotiate, to deal with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't ask any questions about him being authorised. I just came up to him. I recognised him. I said, "Good afternoon." "Good afternoon." He recognised me because he used to come with my brothers up to the house when the house was being built, with the youngest brother. I told him: "Brother, please tell me, what's going on? What's going to happen to us?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he consult anyone, and then afterwards did he then offer you to come for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, "Come." I said, "There are plenty of women and children in my house. I just came here to see. We can all come here to see and you just kill us because we could no longer stay in the house." A friend who lived three or four hundred metres from my house had been killed the night before. And now it was my house's turn. And then he said: "You can all leave, get a white flag, and come here. Something needed to be done." And I don't even remember what day of the week that was. "We'll be here for another one or two days," he told me, "and then no more guarantees because then the army would be there from Serbia. And what will happen to you then, only God knows. But this way, we can offer you some protection at least." That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he offer to take you all for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I never saw him again. I just returned home, and I told the people who were staying in my house "I'm leaving now. And if you want, you can come with me. I don't care about the house." I took my family, and then everyone followed us, all the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he promise to bring you back to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he never said anything, and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the soldier have any insignia, any ranks on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just camouflage uniform and a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of the villagers oppose this agreement of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, everyone agreed, and everyone left because no one could afford to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When people from Hambarine came in June, you talked about that today on page 1936 [as interpreted] of the transcript. You say that for the most part, the group consisted of women and children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And old people, yes. Did they tell you that armed people from Hambarine had withdrawn into the Kurevo forest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Honestly, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did some of them return to Hambarine after a while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Those who left with us went with us to Travnik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 26, I think it is line 22, you say that you left with your son -- actually, with the son of Adem Hopovac who had been killed, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you went to Adem Hopovac's wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: She asked him: "Why did you come?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. "Why did you come, son? Are you hungry?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, are you hungry. Did she know what was going on in Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she knew --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the rest of the answer of the witness. Could it please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. The interpreters didn't manage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Adem Hopovac's wife knew what was happening because there was cleansing in Zecovi on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You offered her to come with you to Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 28, line 2 of today's transcript, you talk about eight dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you informed a man about that and about your need to go to see who these people were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- you mentioned the following: "Maybe they are not from our village."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that around your village, there were some people who were not from that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought it was people from Hambarine, because there were men from Hambarine staying with us, too. It wasn't only women and children. I wasn't that nearby at the first moment; but then the next time again when I returned with these people, I recognised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Serb soldiers come to your village during the day or during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both day and night. During the night, they would go down where they held this checkpoint in the village. They would get drunk, and there they would come drunk. They would shoot during the night, and then we would flee into the forest. During the day, they would go around looting. They took anything they wanted from the houses because they knew that there was no one at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, or rather, did you perhaps hear about this in Travnik or wherever you may have been after that, that in the forest of Kurevo, there was fighting in 1993 as well? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear that there had been some after us, that after we left, that there was some young people who stayed behind, young Muslims. Now whether there actually were some or there weren't any, that, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 39, line 15 of today's transcript, you refer to an incident when Tintar killed Hasib.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far away was Hasib from you when Tintar killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were standing on the left-hand side of the road, and the bridge is on the right-hand side, just sort of across. And then -- and it was like 8 metres, 6 plus 2, yeah, 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated 2000, on page 6, paragraph 7 of the B/C/S version, and the English version is page 6, paragraph 5, you say that "they were 100 metres away."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I'm telling you. I was on one side of the road, and on the other side is the bridge. The man wanted to go into the bus, and Drago Tintar returned him pulling him by the hand this way. And then so the road is 6 metres, and the bridge an additional 2, so it's not only that I could see it; the whole bus could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is recorded in your statement here is not correct; what you told us today is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. [Interpretation] Thank you, madam, for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are there any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to thank you for coming and providing us with your information. Any additional questions by the Judges? That's not the case. Then you are excused for today. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 12.45. And I would ask the parties to be prepared that we go to some documents in List 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. During the break, I heard some rumour that this concludes the case of the Prosecutor. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the week it looks like that way. We don't have another witness this week lined up. We anticipated this witness would take more than a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One and a half hour as you said, correctly. Extremely precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Waidyaratne is very accurate, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I ask, indeed, we can't proceed this way, to be serious. What is expected, at least by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We don't have a witness lined up for tomorrow. We could, if we start calling -- all of our witnesses live in other countries. We don't have any left that live in this country, with the possible exception of part of the demographer's -- the demographer has been out of town, but I think is back today. Part of he demographer's evidence we might be able to call tomorrow, but I have to check and see if she did return today. And I don't know if the Defence is ready to do that cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What Mr. Inayat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat is here, but what remains for him to testify to is the sourcing of all the documents. We haven't put in all the documents yet. One thing I could do by tomorrow, this afternoon, is go through and find many, if not all the rest, many more of the documents that we intend to introduce and at least introduce them. I don't know if the Court actually wants to read those tomorrow, but we could do that. But personally I don't think it would be productive to have Mr. Inayat testify again only partially because he will have to testify when we have completed all of our documents coming into evidence as to the sourcing of all the documents. If Your Honours wish to have him testify tomorrow and then again later in the case, that could be done. But also, Mr. Ostojic had started the cross-examination, and he's not here this week. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the entire week not here. Okay. But sorry to say, we have to proceed, and we can't stop once again an entire day, and therefore I would ask the OTP to take care to do what is possible as regards witnesses or experts being in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, the only expert report that's prepared and disclosed would be the demographer. And actually that is being revised. However half of it is done that's the demographer. I have asked for a revision because that report is several years old, and the data now is much more precise as to the total number missing, killed and exhumed during the relevant period. I know part of the reason that that report is not done is because we had anticipated getting this latest version of the book of missing persons electronically which we were supposed to get by the -- they said at the earliest by the end of June, but that has not yet arrived. So that's what's holding that up, but I could check with her and see if she is available tomorrow if Mr. Lukic is prepared to cross-examine her, or I could at least put on her direct examination. Excuse me, Ms. Karper tells me that that report has not been disclosed, but this is one that was disclosed before the trial began. Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the report is not yet disclosed, then indeed I don't dare even to ask the Defence whether or not they are prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that we are not prepared, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For understandable reasons; we haven't disclosed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore, it remains to proceed with Mr. Inayat step by step, and I have to ask the OTP to be prepared that we can hear Mr. Inayat at least the next step of introducing documents the OTP believes are of utmost relevance and they want to introduce into the case as soon as possible. So therefore, we should start tomorrow early doing this. But before we come to this point, then tomorrow, I think we have to go through what we have as documents and what is still missing. First, I recall that Witness Minka Cehajic told us that she would send us a letter by fax, and this fax has arrived as it was in the courtroom, and is this document now prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the document. I'm not sure that the translation is back yet, but we can check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you please could be so kind and check it also for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, also this morning, Your Honour mentioned List 4. We have that to be distributed, or perhaps it has been distributed. We have it here to be distributed, and perhaps that could be given an exhibit number to be marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. Feel free to distribute this. And I understand it would be in exchange of the list we had starting with S172. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, this goes from S172 through S179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In addition, one other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think that we need a new exhibit number; we just exchange this as first pages of List 4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the initial List 4 was not marked, so shall we assign a number now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have special binders, list called List 4, and after that we have the documents from 172 until 179. It's just as a kind of cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One other minor matter, some week or two ago, I was given a diagram of the courtroom layout where it has been marked, someone has marked 97 square metres. I think I had asked if the Court could put on the record some kind of estimate of the size of the courtroom because witnesses have referred to this courtroom in comparing it to the facilities in which they were detained. Could the Court make that estimate, or would the Defence counsel agree to that, that this courtroom contains approximately 97 square metres in space?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and let the usher bring this document to the Defence and then to the Bench. Thank you. If the OTP could be so kind and give a copy to the parties and to the Judges, and then we would have this as a formal exhibit. I can't see any objections. This would then be S189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Regarding copies, that is what I received from -- I thought it was from Your Honours I received that. Okay, I guess from the Registry I received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then before turning to other documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have the colour copies that Your Honours requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, apparently. We think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If they could be distributed, please, and once again, let's take them under the exhibit numbers we have already adduced to these documents, only additional -1 in each case. Thank you. Then on the documents, the missing translation I mentioned this morning was on Document S151 A. This was a videotape with Witness Sejmenovic, and here we had only a mixture of English and B/C/S already. And a kind of draft translation. This was missing. And I take it that -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That has been submitted to CLSS for a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then as regards Document 157, transcripts would be appreciated. It was a press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get transcripts of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we need a translation of Document S44 B. This was a letter from a witness. I think it was Witness A. Right? It was already from the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was Mr. Murselovic, not Witness A, who provided a dismissal, if I recall correctly, it was. He had a copy, but we also had a copy which I believe is S45 that has been translated. So I think there was some issue about his copy, how he got it, and he indicated that both the front and back were on one paper when he first photocopied it. But S45, I believe, I have been told, is the same as S44 and is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Then we have still open a motion filed by the Defence substituting a former motion under Rule 95. We asked for observations by the OTP due for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I know I made a draft, and apparently it's not yet filed. So when it has been slightly revised, but it will be filed -- is it ready now? I'll ask that it be brought down. Certainly it's very close to being filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then for the following exercise, I need to a certain extent the assistance of the OTP, especially one may to say to disclose what are the documents they regard as of such an outstanding importance that they need to be read out in addition? I take it that the documents S59 and following are already read out, but not S81, if the list of the Registry gives me the correct answers. S81.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 65 ter 257, for the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be one that we think is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid it was not read out because we didn't have it before us at that day. May I ask the Registry to read out this in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "/handwritten: Simo Markovic/Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina/handwritten 49/Krajina autonomous region/handwritten:/? 50/Prijedor Municipality. Crisis Staff. "Number: 02-111-237/92. "Date: 23 June, 1992. "Pursuant to Articles 3 and 7 of the decision on the organisation and work of the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff, the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff at a session held on 23 June, 1992, took the following decision: "One, it is forbidden to use funds from the accounts of economic enterprises and independent shops whose owners were killed, have moved away, or were arrested for armed intervention. "Two, approval is hereby given for the municipal secretariat for the economy to temporarily use the funds in the giro accounts of the/people/referred to in the preceding paragraph in the form of a loan. "Three, the Prijedor SDK/public auditing service/and the municipal secretariat of the economy shall see to the implementation of this decision. "Four, this decision comes into effect on the day it is adopted. "Delivered to: One, Prijedor SDK; two, municipal secretariat for the economy; three, files. "/Handwritten: For/president of the Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic./signature and stamped/".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This brings me to a former request as regards an overview on the interrelationship amongst the documents presented by the OTP. And I would be grateful if the OTP in this context could provide us with a synopsis showing which of these documents we have here before us were published in the Official Gazette of Prijedor we have before us as S180 and S181.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's already been assigned to someone to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, what about S90? According to the list before me, it was not yet read out. This may be due to the fact that at that time, we read out in context documents bearing a kind of signature at least. And here, we don't have any. Therefore, this document should be read out knowing that on that what is called the original, there is no signature at all. But could it be read out now. It was the former 65 ter, number 365.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Minutes of the session of the National Defence Council of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly held at 1200 hours on 29th September, 1992 in the offices of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. The session was presided over by Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the council. The session was attended by: Dr. Milomir Stakic, Dragan Savanovic, Dr. Milan Kovacevic, Radmilo Zeljaja, Bosko Mandic, Slavko Budimir, Ranko Travar, Simo Drljaca, and Miljenko Rajlic. The minutes were taken by Spiro Marmat. The following agenda was agreed for this session. "Agenda, 1, discussion about the minutes of the previous session of the National Defence Council. " 2, report on the forthcoming activities regarding the open Trnopolje reception centre. "3, ensuring an adequate number of teachers for the normal work of the schools. "Item 1: Discussion of the minutes of the previous session of the National Defence Council. "After the discussion, the following was concluded: 1, the minutes of the previous session of the National Defence Council were approved. Item 2: Report on the forthcoming activities regarding the open Trnopolje reception centre. After the discussion, the following was concluded: 1, the National Defence Council will take on all the essential obligations regarding the unhindered arrival of all persons from the open Trnopolje reception centre according to a list agreed by the Municipal Red Cross and the International Red Cross. "2, the public security station in Prijedor will provide escort for the convoy and the secretariat for the economy and social services will provide vehicles and fuel. "3, the Municipal Red Cross will be advised to close down the open Trnopolje reception as the departure of all registered persons from this reception centre effectively makes it unnecessary. "Item 3, ensuring an adequate number of teachers for the normal work of the schools. After the discussion, the following was concluded: 1, it was recommended by to the army command that it agree on the requirements with the school directors on the basis of written requests and to exempt from military service all teachers essential for the normal teaching process. "It was also concluded that: 1, the 3.000 liters of petrol [Regular] which has arrived to be distributed to the battalion commands to meet the requirements of their soldiers. Petrol requirements by battalions will be determined by the tactical group command. "The chairman closed the session at 1330 hours. "Minutes taken by Spiro Marmat. "President of the National Defence Council, Dr. Milomir Stakic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the translation does not indicate it, but looking at the original, I think it should be noted that it indicates "Stakic, Dr. Milomir, SR" We had some testimony about what that meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional remark. May we then turn to the former 65 ter number 455, which is now S92. Do you need another copy?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Supplement to instructions on the establishment, composition, and tasks of area Crisis Staffs in Prijedor Municipality. "2, vice-president of the Crisis Substaff;. "3, assistant to the president for civilian protection;. "4, assistant to the president for political work and information; and. "5, assistant to the president for logistics. "Apart from establishing working groups, commissions, and other working bodies for specific tasks, the Crisis Substaffs shall also appoint the following permanent officers: Supply officer, officer for quartermaster support, officer for transport and technical support, purchasing officer, health-care officer. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "The work of these officers shall be directed, coordinated, and directly managed by the assistant to the president for logistics. "II: The provisions of instructions on the establishment, composition, and tasks of area Crisis Substaffs in Prijedor Municipality shall by extension apply to the work of Crisis Substaffs in accordance with their area of competence/as printed/" "President of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality, Milomir Stakic/stamped/".

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think Your Honour anticipates, I'd like to make the same observation on this document except to note that while the last one was written in Latin script, this document is written in Cyrillic. And again, next to the name of "Milomir Stakic" appear the Cyrillic letters SR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. May I turn to the document I just had, this was the former 65 ter number 440. And on purpose, I didn't take it as it is. Does the OTP have the original radio tape in its possession?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think we do, I'll check on that. For the Court's information, I believe that we seized, the during one of the searches, nine radio tapes. This is one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because here, we have to go back to the most original document. And in this case, it would be the tape, and the tape would have to be played. Could this be done tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We also have the motion -- the response to the defendant Stakic's motion to bar and exclude evidence regarding the testimony of Mr. Sejmenovic. That is already to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and read it out so that we have immediately the access in French also. Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It has not been filed yet, but it will be. Your Honour, it's filed as confidential, because there's a portion of it that was confidential in the Defence motion.
